# Invention as a method (organised research and development) (`systematic_invention`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, measurement_quantification, patents, industrial_research_lab
- Core idea: Inventions can be produced on purpose instead of waiting for luck or genius: state the need as a measurable target, collect what is already known, build small cheap models, vary one feature at a time and measure the result, keep a notebook of every trial including failures, and put people with different skills (a mathematician, a smith, a glassmaker) in one workshop with money and time. Smeaton found the best waterwheel in 1759 by testing model wheels on a bench; Edison's team tried thousands of filament materials; the Wright brothers tested about 200 wing shapes in a wind tunnel before building. The method needs a patron who accepts that most trials fail and is paid back by the few that work.
- Pitfalls:
  - The lone-genius and 'eureka' story; Edison ran a staffed laboratory and did not invent the light bulb from nothing (Swan and others preceded him)
  - Blind trial and error without measurement or theory, which wastes years
  - Testing at full scale first; a failed full-size engine or bridge ends the patronage
  - Assuming an invention that works will be adopted; it must also be cheaper or better than what guilds and users already have
- History: egypt: 3rd c. BC – Ptolemaic Alexandria funds engineers who, by systematic trials, find the formula relating a catapult's spring diameter to its shot (reported by Philo of Byzantium, c. 200 BC); china: Han to Song – state workshops and arsenals with recorded specifications; improvement is organised but not as open-ended research; islamic: 1259 Maragha and 1420s Samarkand observatories as funded research institutes with staff, instruments and libraries; europe: 1576 – Tycho's Uraniborg; 1627 Bacon's fictional 'Salomon's House'; 1714 Longitude prize; 1759 Smeaton's model experiments; 1826 Liebig's teaching laboratory at Giessen; 1870s–1880s German dye-industry laboratories; americas: 1876 – Edison's Menlo Park laboratory; 1900 General Electric Research Laboratory; 1901 Wright brothers' wind tunnel; 1925 Bell Telephone Laboratories
- Read:
  - Alfred North Whitehead, Science and the Modern World (1925)
  - Thomas P. Hughes, American Genesis: A Century of Invention and Technological Enthusiasm, 1870–1970 (1989)
  - Jon Gertner, The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation (2012)
